Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyy Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi, Ukraine

Not demolished. The earliest evidence of this cemetery dates to the first half of the 19th century; per the Russian Jewish Encyclopedia, its oldest tombstone dates to 1821 (the ESJF team itself found one from 1828), and it appears on city plans from 1841. It's unknown whether this was the city's first Jewish cemetery, or where the earlier pre-Russian-era Akkerman Jewish cemetery stood; it was reportedly heavily damaged during WWII but remains operational today. Jews are first mentioned in the city in 1330, arriving in greater numbers after the 1492 Spanish expulsion; a Karaite community existed from the early 16th century. A Hevra Kadisha formed by 1807; population reached 413 by 1827, with two synagogues by mid-century. A pogrom struck in 1865; a Jewish hospital and Talmud Torah opened in 1882, followed by a Sabbath school and Zionist activity (including Hovevei Zion, one of the city's earliest Zionist organizations) by century's end. Population reached 5,624 (20%) by 1897; an October 17, 1905 pogrom killed eight Jews. By 1910, six synagogues, a poor-relief charity, and four vocational schools operated. Post-1917 Revolution saw the Tzeirei Zion organization emerge alongside a democratic Jewish community, Zionist library, and Hebrew kindergarten; population reached about 8,000 by 1940. Soviet rule closed Jewish organizations and arrested their leaders; ten Jewish families were deported to Siberia on June 13, 1941, and many young Jews were called to Red Army service. Nazi occupation from July 28, 1941 saw nearly 3,000 Jews executed between July-September that year; the remaining 55 were expelled to Transnistria that September. About 250 Jews returned after the war.
